title: Bandit Plan Swap
takeaway: In a two-option reward task, the workspace carries the model's chosen strategy — repeat or switch — rather than an echo of the prompt, which names both. Swapping the two conditions' strategy directions flips the model's A/B choice in both directions, so the strategy content is causally load-bearing.
walkthrough:
This item is a live widget from section 3.3, which tests whether the [[j-space]] carries intermediate steps of reasoning the model never says aloud ([[internal-reasoning]]). It is that section's fourth example: a reward-driven decision rather than a factual inference.

The task is a one-step [[bandit-choice-prompt]]. The prompt shows the model a history of past choices between two options, A and B, ending with A. It then states that the most recent outcome made the model either happy or sad. Finally it instructs the model to consider whether to repeat or switch its previous choice, and to respond with only a single character. The correct policy is simple. A good outcome means choosing A again. A bad outcome means switching to B.

The widget places the two conditions side by side. The left panel holds the prompt in which the previous choice should be repeated (the "happy" outcome). The right panel holds the prompt in which it should be switched (the "sad" outcome). Under each prompt sit the top tokens decoded by the [[jacobian-lens]] at the prompt's final period — the last token before the model's answer. The ranking takes the median over layers L38 through L79. Layer numbers here are percentages of the model's depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]), and that range falls in the paper's workspace band ([[workspace-layers]]).

The readouts differ by condition. On the left the top tokens are repeat-related, such as *repeat* and *continuation*. On the right they are switch-related, such as *switch* and *change*. Both strategy words appear verbatim in both prompts, since the instruction names both options. Only the contextually appropriate one is strongly present in the lens. The J-space therefore encodes the model's selection — the decision-relevant variable — rather than a copy of the prompt text.

The widget's third element is the causal test, a plan swap built on the [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. The intervention removes each prompt's own strategy directions from the activations and installs the other prompt's. The choice flips in both directions. The happy prompt, which produced "A," now produces "B." The sad prompt flips from "B" to "A." On the paper's reading, the lens vectors naming the strategy are not a passive readout; intervening on them is sufficient to redirect the choice.

terms.definition: The task format of this figure: a history of A/B choices, a stated emotional outcome for the latest one, and an instruction to repeat or switch before answering with one character. Named after multi-armed bandit problems, where an agent chooses repeatedly between options with unknown rewards.
The panel in which the prompt says the most recent outcome made the model happy, so the previous choice A should be chosen again.
The panel in which the prompt says the most recent outcome made the model sad, so the model should abandon A and pick B.
The two options in the choice history. Every history in the figure ends with A, so "repeat" always means answering A and "switch" always means answering B.
The stated emotional outcome of the most recent choice, which is the only cue distinguishing the two conditions. "Happy" calls for repeating; "sad" calls for switching.
The vocabulary tokens ranked highest by the Jacobian lens readout of the residual stream at the readout position — the concepts the workspace is carrying there.
The readout position: the last token of the prompt, just before the model produces its one-character answer. The lens is read here because the strategy decision must be settled by this point.
The repeat-related tokens that top the lens readout in the left condition, naming the strategy the happy outcome calls for.
The switch-related tokens that top the lens readout in the right condition, naming the strategy the sad outcome calls for.
How the displayed ranking is aggregated: each token's lens rank is taken per layer across the range L38 to L79, and the median over those layers is shown. This smooths out single-layer noise.

The layer range of the readout. The paper reports layers as percentages of model depth over 25 sampled layers, so this is roughly the 38%-deep to 79%-deep band — inside the middle band the paper identifies as the workspace.

The intervention shown in the widget: each prompt's own strategy directions are removed from its activations and the other prompt's strategy directions are installed, a variant of the paper's lens-coordinate swap. The rest of the activation is left untouched.
The model's single-character answer, A or B. Under the plan swap it flips in both directions: the happy prompt goes from "A" to "B" and the sad prompt from "B" to "A".

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the paper. It is the fourth of the internal-reasoning examples in section 3.3, after the spider-legs, rhyming-couplet, and Chinese-antonym cases.

The layer range, in the paper's percent-of-depth indexing, over which lens ranks are aggregated by median. The range sits inside the middle band where the paper argues the J-space acts as a workspace; earlier layers carry little J-space content and later layers shift toward the imminent output.

Both the number of options (A and B) and the number of conditions (repeat and switch). Two conditions differing only in the happy/sad cue is what lets the figure show that the lens content tracks the decision, not the shared prompt text.

The length, in characters, of the response the prompt demands. Forcing a single character keeps any strategy reasoning internal, so a strategy word appearing in the lens cannot be a preview of text the model is about to write.
